# Hive Structure

The honey bee hive is built from hexagonal wax cells arranged in parallel
combs. Worker bees secrete wax from glands on their abdomen and shape it
with their mandibles. Brood cells in the centre of the comb hold eggs and
larvae, while the outer cells store pollen and honey. A beekeeper inspects
the frames of a Langstroth hive by lifting them one at a time and checking
the brood pattern for gaps that may signal disease. A healthy colony will
raise a new queen within days when the old queen is lost, feeding chosen
larvae a diet of royal jelly. Propolis, a resin gathered from tree buds,
seals cracks in the hive and protects the colony against microbes.

# Honey Harvest

Honey is harvested in late summer when the supers are full and the cells are
capped with wax. The beekeeper removes the frames, slices the wax cappings
with a heated knife, and spins the frames in a centrifugal extractor. Raw
honey is strained through a fine mesh to remove wax fragments before
bottling. Enough honey must always be left in the hive so the colony can
survive the winter, since bees cluster together and eat stored honey to
generate heat during cold months when no nectar is available.

# Swarming

Swarming is how a honey bee colony reproduces. When the hive becomes
crowded, the old queen leaves with roughly half of the workers and settles
temporarily on a branch while scout bees search for a new nest site. Scouts
perform waggle dances to advertise candidate cavities, and the swarm departs
once a quorum of scouts agrees on one location. Beekeepers prevent swarming
by giving the colony more room, splitting strong hives, and removing queen
cells during the spring buildup.
